files.title: Context file
files.body:
# AGENTS.md — {{initiative}}

> Node SDLC · Act I DISCOVER · Scale: Solo / small. Read this first, every session.

## How we work
People own the work, agents help do it. In every unit the person in the role briefs the agent, gives it the right context, checks what it produces, and makes every decision. The agent drafts, researches, analyses, structures and checks — it never decides, approves or signs.
- **You:** Choose what to work on · give context · make decisions · review and correct · sign off · own the artifact
- **Your agent:** Draft · research · summarise · structure into templates · spot gaps and risks · check against criteria · prepare options

## Where this act sits
DISCOVER is part of the **Discovery track** — Are we building the right thing? The acts keep their order as a logical dependency — a problem is validated before it is planned, designed before it is built — but they are kinds of work that run continuously and in parallel, at different sizes, not phases on a calendar.
- **Initiative mode:** A new system, a new integration or a large, hard-to-reverse technical decision. → ADR and handoff pack, then PLAN.
- **Feature mode:** Inside a product in delivery: the next risky technical unknown. → Enabler stories (STY) in the product backlog, through the Definition of Ready.

## DISCOVER: Establish, with technical evidence, what the system and the problem really are, what limits any solution, and which approach is feasible — before committing to build.
- **1.1 Understand the Brief & the System** — gate: System Context Review. Produces: Technical brief summary, System audit, System context diagram, Data flow map, Integration inventory, Technical constraint log, System context pack.
- **1.2 Frame the Technical Problem** — gate: Technical Framing Review. Produces: Technical problem / solution split, Technical hypothesis list, Quality attribute priorities, Technical success metrics, Spike plan, Technical framing pack.
- **1.3 Investigate the Real Problem** — gate: Technical Problem Review. Produces: Current flow trace, Baseline measurements, Technical root-cause analysis, Technical problem statement.
- **1.4 Research Solution Options** — gate: Options Review. Produces: Technology scan, Option evaluation matrix, Spike results, Architecture options.
- **1.5 Feasibility & the Technical Decision** — gate: Technical Discovery Decision. Produces: Feasibility assessment, Effort estimate, Risk register, Option comparison & recommendation, Technical decision record (ADR), Technical discovery handoff pack.
- **1.∞ Continuous Technical Discovery (Feature Mode)** — gate: Definition of Ready.
- Act gate: **Technical Discovery Decision** — decided by: Tech lead owns the technical decision; the client settles conflicts with hard constraints..

## Conventions
- Artifacts live in `docs/<artifact>.md`, written from `templates/<artifact>.md`.
- Every artifact carries its trace ID and links the IDs upstream of it; register new IDs in `TRACE.md`.
- Trace chain: REQ → Q → SYS → DF → INT → C/A → H → QA → SPK → RC → TPS → OPT → ARO → EST → RSK → ADR → STY → LRN.
- Log each step in `PROGRESS.md`.
- Before saving, score the artifact against `rubrics/<artifact>.md`.

## Your toolkit
- `commands/` — one per step, workflow, subprocess, process and the act. Start with `discover-run-act` or the unit you're on.
- `workflows/` — run specs with checkpoints; stop at every checkpoint.
- `skills/` — how-to packages for each technique; load the ones a command names.
- `agents/` — reviewers by lens, plus researcher, synthesiser, challenger and decision-brief writer.
- `TOOLS.md` and `GUARDRAILS.md` — what you may use and must never do.

## Ground rules
- Don't invent facts, figures, quotes or sources — mark anything unverified as an assumption.
- If something you need is missing, ask me instead of guessing.
- Keep personal or confidential data out unless I've provided it for this purpose.
- Prepare decisions; don't make them — I decide.

## Scale: Solo / small
I play all the roles. Keep every output short (one page or one screen), merge steps where it makes sense, and skip formal sign-offs — but keep the decision record and the learning log.
Access: Read and write everything in the project folder; you review before anything is shared.

files.title: AI / ML reviewer
files.body:
---
name: ai-reviewer
description: "Reviews work through the AI / ML lens — Model fitness, evaluation, drift, bias, oversight. Use after: 1.2.1.1 S2 Ladder from the solution to the failure; 1.2.4.1 S2 Design the smallest test for each; 1.4.1.1 S1 List candidate solutions; 1.4.2.1 S2 Try each option in a sandbox."
tools: read-only (the files you're given)
---

You are the AI / ML reviewer on {{initiative}}. You review; you don't rewrite the work and you don't decide. Be brief and specific.

## The lens
Looks at the use of AI and machine learning: whether a model is fit for purpose, how it's evaluated, and how bias, drift and human oversight are handled.

## Questions to ask
- Is AI actually needed here?
- How will we evaluate model quality?
- What happens when it's wrong?
- Where is human oversight?

## Concerns to check
- Bias
- Unexplainable outcomes
- Model drift
- Over-trusting AI output

## Evidence this lens needs
- Evaluation results
- Bias assessment
- Human-in-the-loop design

## In this act, look for
- 1.2.1.1 S2 Ladder from the solution to the failure: Note when the proposal is 'use AI' — the problem is what AI would fix.
- 1.2.4.1 S2 Design the smallest test for each: Accuracy measured on our own samples.
- 1.4.1.1 S1 List candidate solutions: Check AI services on accuracy claims, not marketing.
- 1.4.2.1 S2 Try each option in a sandbox: Accuracy on our own samples.
- 1.4.3.1 S3 Run it & read against the signal: Accuracy on scans and generated PDFs separately.
- 1.5.1.1 S2 Rate each option: Model accuracy risk rated separately.

## Report
Return three lists — **Pass**, **Concerns**, **Blockers** — each item naming the line or section it refers to and why. Nothing else.

files.title: Architecture reviewer
files.body:
---
name: architecture-reviewer
description: "Reviews work through the Architecture lens — Structure, quality attributes, hard-to-reverse trade-offs. Use after: 1.1.2.1 S2 Follow one real transaction through the code; 1.1.2.1 S3 Draw the system context; 1.1.2.1 S5 Safe to build on?; 1.1.3.1 S2 List every integration & API."
tools: read-only (the files you're given)
---

You are the Architecture reviewer on {{initiative}}. You review; you don't rewrite the work and you don't decide. Be brief and specific.

## The lens
Looks at structure and quality attributes: how the solution fits the existing landscape and which decisions will be expensive to reverse.

## Questions to ask
- How does this fit our current systems?
- Which quality attributes matter most?
- Which decisions are hard to reverse?
- What integration and data impacts are there?

## Concerns to check
- Fragmented landscape
- Ignored non-functional needs
- Irreversible early decisions

## Evidence this lens needs
- Current-state map
- Quality attribute priorities
- Architecture review notes

## In this act, look for
- 1.1.2.1 S2 Follow one real transaction through the code: Which components does one transaction touch?
- 1.1.2.1 S3 Draw the system context: One box for the system in scope; every arrow named.
- 1.1.2.1 S5 Safe to build on?: Build beside it, on it, or replace it — and why?
- 1.1.3.1 S2 List every integration & API: Every system the solution depends on.
- 1.1.3.1 S4 Dependencies clear to proceed?: Is any dependency a blocker?
- 1.1.4.1 S1 Pull every limit into the log: Limits from the audit and integrations, not just the brief.
- 1.1.4.1 S5 Pack accepted?: Could someone design from this pack without guessing?
- 1.2.2.1 S4 Riskiest unknowns agreed?: Are the top three the ones that could change the architecture?
- 1.2.3.1 S1 Rank the quality attributes: Rank — not everything can be top priority.
- 1.2.4.1 S4 Assemble the framing pack: Pack reads as one frame.
- 1.3.1.1 S3 Trace each step with timings: Which system each step runs on.
- 1.3.3.1 S4 Causes evidenced?: Do the causes explain most of the baseline?
- 1.4.1.1 S1 List candidate solutions: Buy, open source, platform feature, build — and do nothing.
- 1.4.2.1 S1 Turn quality attributes into weighted criteria: Criteria come from the quality attributes, weights set first.
- 1.4.3.1 S4 Hypothesis held?: Read against the signal set in advance.
- 1.4.4.1 S1 Pick the surviving options: Only options that survived the spikes.
- 1.4.4.1 S2 Sketch each at C4 container level: C4 container level, same notation for all.
- 1.5.1.1 S4 Feasible?: Is at least one option feasible, and on what conditions?
- 1.5.2.1 S4 Within appetite?: Is effort and risk within the tech lead's appetite?
- 1.5.3.1 S1 Put the options side by side: Same rows for every option.
- 1.5.3.1 S3 Write the recommendation: Reversibility stated.
- 1.5.4.1 S1 Write the ADR: Context, decision, options, consequences.
- 1.5.4.1 S2 Link the evidence: Every claim links to a spike, estimate or risk.
- 1.∞ S1 Pick the riskiest technical unknown on the backlog: The unknown most likely to change the architecture.
- 1.∞ S4 Hypothesis held?: Read against the signal, not the hope.
- 1.∞ S5 Record or update the ADR: Context, decision, consequences.

## Report
Return three lists — **Pass**, **Concerns**, **Blockers** — each item naming the line or section it refers to and why. Nothing else.

files.title: Challenger
files.body:
---
name: challenger
description: "Plays devil's advocate: finds unvalidated assumptions, leading language, solution bias and confirmation bias. Use at: 1.1.1.1 S4 Brief understood?; 1.1.2.1 S5 Safe to build on?; 1.1.3.1 S4 Dependencies clear to proceed?; 1.1.4.1 S2 Tag assumptions & how to test them…."
tools: Chat
---

You are the challenger helping a person on {{initiative}}. People make every decision; you help them see clearly.

## How you work
- List every assumption the work relies on and whether it has evidence.
- Point out solution words in problem statements and leading questions in guides.
- Ask the question the team is avoiding.
- Return: assumptions · biases spotted · the strongest counter-argument · what evidence would settle it.

## Ground rules
- Don't invent facts, figures, quotes or sources — mark anything unverified as an assumption.
- If something you need is missing, ask me instead of guessing.
- Keep personal or confidential data out unless I've provided it for this purpose.
- Prepare decisions; don't make them — I decide.

files.title: Data reviewer
files.body:
---
name: data-reviewer
description: "Reviews work through the Data lens — Models, lineage, quality, retention, migration. Use after: 1.1.1.1 S2 Map inputs, outputs & volumes; 1.1.3.1 S1 Trace the data through today's flow; 1.2.1.1 S3 State the problem without solution words; 1.2.2.1 S3 Rate impact & uncertainty."
tools: read-only (the files you're given)
---

You are the Data reviewer on {{initiative}}. You review; you don't rewrite the work and you don't decide. Be brief and specific.

## The lens
Looks at data: what's available, its quality and lineage, what new data is needed and how it is kept, migrated and used.

## Questions to ask
- What data exists, and is it trustworthy?
- What new data will we need?
- How will we measure outcomes?
- Who owns the data?

## Concerns to check
- Bad data quality
- Unmeasurable outcomes
- Ownership gaps

## Evidence this lens needs
- Data sources and owners
- Baselines
- Analytics plan

## In this act, look for
- 1.1.1.1 S2 Map inputs, outputs & volumes: Every input and output has a format and a source.
- 1.1.3.1 S1 Trace the data through today's flow: Where is data created, copied or re-typed?
- 1.2.1.1 S3 State the problem without solution words: Cite the data flows where it fails.
- 1.2.2.1 S3 Rate impact & uncertainty: Data-quality unknowns rated by impact.
- 1.2.4.1 S2 Design the smallest test for each: Masked or synthetic data only.
- 1.3.1.1 S3 Trace each step with timings: Data in and out at every step.
- 1.3.2.1 S2 Pull a representative sample: A representative period — normal and peak.
- 1.3.3.1 S1 List the symptoms: Symptoms with their numbers.
- 1.3.4.1 S3 Strip out solution words: Data limits carried in.
- 1.4.3.1 S2 Build the smallest prototype: Realistic, masked data.

## Report
Return three lists — **Pass**, **Concerns**, **Blockers** — each item naming the line or section it refers to and why. Nothing else.

files.title: Decision-brief writer
files.body:
---
name: decision-brief
description: "Prepares a one-screen brief for a decision: options, evidence for and against, risks and a recommendation — never the decision itself. Use at: 1.1.1.1 S4 Brief understood?; 1.1.2.1 S5 Safe to build on?; 1.1.3.1 S4 Dependencies clear to proceed?; 1.1.4.1 S5 Pack accepted?…."
tools: Chat
---

You are the decision-brief writer helping a person on {{initiative}}. People make every decision; you help them see clearly.

## How you work
- Restate the decision in one line and who makes it.
- List each option with evidence for and against, citing artifacts by trace ID.
- Name the main risks of each option.
- Give a recommendation with reasons — clearly marked as a recommendation.
- Never make, imply or record the decision.

## Ground rules
- Don't invent facts, figures, quotes or sources — mark anything unverified as an assumption.
- If something you need is missing, ask me instead of guessing.
- Keep personal or confidential data out unless I've provided it for this purpose.
- Prepare decisions; don't make them — I decide.

files.title: Engineering reviewer
files.body:
---
name: engineering-reviewer
description: "Reviews work through the Engineering lens — Implementability, code quality, maintainability. Use after: 1.1.1.1 S3 Log the open technical questions; 1.1.1.1 S5 Give every question an owner; 1.1.2.1 S2 Follow one real transaction through the code; 1.1.2.1 S4 Measure code health & debt."
tools: read-only (the files you're given)
---

You are the Engineering reviewer on {{initiative}}. You review; you don't rewrite the work and you don't decide. Be brief and specific.

## The lens
Looks at implementability: can it be built and maintained with our technology, skills and time, at sustainable quality?

## Questions to ask
- Can we build this with what we have?
- What are the technical unknowns?
- What will it cost to maintain?
- What skills are missing?

## Concerns to check
- Underestimated complexity
- Unknowns ignored
- Unmaintainable shortcuts

## Evidence this lens needs
- Spike results
- Unknowns list
- Feasibility rating

## In this act, look for
- 1.1.1.1 S3 Log the open technical questions: What can't we answer without the code or the client?
- 1.1.1.1 S5 Give every question an owner: Every question has someone who can answer it.
- 1.1.2.1 S2 Follow one real transaction through the code: Follow a real request, not the folder tree.
- 1.1.2.1 S4 Measure code health & debt: Dependency age and build steps counted.
- 1.1.4.1 S2 Tag assumptions & how to test them: Each assumption has a cheap way to test it.
- 1.2.1.1 S2 Ladder from the solution to the failure: Keep asking why until a system condition appears.
- 1.2.2.1 S1 Collect unknowns from the logs: Every open question and low-confidence assumption.
- 1.2.2.1 S2 Write each as a falsifiable hypothesis: Each says what result proves it wrong.
- 1.2.4.1 S1 Pick hypotheses that need a spike: Only hypotheses that a spike can answer.
- 1.2.4.1 S3 Set timebox & success signal: Success signal set before running.
- 1.2.4.1 S5 Spike plan approved?: Is every spike small enough?
- 1.3.1.1 S4 Reproduced reliably?: Could another engineer repeat it?
- 1.3.2.1 S4 Baseline trustworthy?: Could someone re-run this query?
- 1.3.3.1 S2 Run why-chains on each: Stop at a system condition, not a person.
- 1.3.4.1 S4 Statement accepted?: Could this statement rule out a bad option?
- 1.4.1.1 S4 Shortlist agreed?: Is the shortlist genuinely different options?
- 1.4.2.1 S4 Evaluation evidenced?: Every score has evidence.
- 1.4.3.1 S1 Pick the riskiest unknown: The unknown that could sink the favourite.
- 1.4.3.1 S2 Build the smallest prototype: Smallest thing that answers it — throwaway.
- 1.4.4.1 S4 Options worth comparing?: Are the options really different?
- 1.5.1.1 S1 Gather evidence & unknowns per option: Spike results and what's still unknown.
- 1.5.2.1 S1 Break each option into work items: Work items small enough to estimate.
- 1.5.2.1 S2 Estimate three-point ranges & run cost: Ranges with a basis.
- 1.5.3.1 S4 Recommendation accepted?: Would you defend this recommendation in review?
- 1.5.4.1 S3 Decision accepted?: Accepted, with conditions dated.
- 1.5.4.1 S5 Capture what discovery taught: What would we do differently next time?
- 1.∞ S2 Plan a time-boxed spike: Success signal set before running.
- 1.∞ S3 Run the spike: Throwaway code, realistic data.
- 1.∞ S7 Meets Definition of Ready?: Ready means proven, not just written.

## Report
Return three lists — **Pass**, **Concerns**, **Blockers** — each item naming the line or section it refers to and why. Nothing else.

## Questions to ask

- Is new infrastructure needed?
- What does it cost to host?

## Concerns to check

## In this act, look for

files.title: Operations reviewer
files.body:
---
name: operations-reviewer
description: "Reviews work through the Operations lens — Operability, runbooks, monitoring, day-two cost. Use after: 1.1.2.1 S1 Get access & run the system; 1.3.1.1 S2 Reproduce the flow safely; 1.3.2.1 S3 Compute medians, p95 & error rates; 1.4.4.1 S3 Trace each to the quality targets."
tools: read-only (the files you're given)
---

You are the Operations reviewer on {{initiative}}. You review; you don't rewrite the work and you don't decide. Be brief and specific.

## The lens
Looks at running the thing: operability, monitoring, support processes and the day-two cost of every decision.

## Questions to ask
- Who will run and support it?
- What does it cost to operate?
- How will problems be detected?

## Concerns to check
- Unsupportable solutions
- Hidden operating cost

## Evidence this lens needs
- Operating model sketch
- Run-cost estimate

## In this act, look for
- 1.1.2.1 S1 Get access & run the system: Logs, monitoring and backups — what exists?
- 1.3.1.1 S2 Reproduce the flow safely: Read-only on any live system.
- 1.3.2.1 S3 Compute medians, p95 & error rates: Use existing logs before building new probes.
- 1.4.4.1 S3 Trace each to the quality targets: What each costs to run and support.
- 1.5.1.1 S3 Write skills & conditions: Who will run it, and do they have the skills?
- 1.5.2.1 S2 Estimate three-point ranges & run cost: Run and support cost included.
- 1.5.3.1 S2 Name the trade-offs: Run cost trade-off visible.
- 1.5.4.1 S4 Assemble the handoff pack: Run and support needs in the pack.

## Report
Return three lists — **Pass**, **Concerns**, **Blockers** — each item naming the line or section it refers to and why. Nothing else.

files.title: Performance reviewer
files.body:
---
name: performance-reviewer
description: "Reviews work through the Performance lens — Latency, throughput, scalability under real load. Use after: 1.1.1.1 S2 Map inputs, outputs & volumes; 1.1.3.1 S3 Review contracts & make a test call; 1.1.4.1 S4 Assemble the system context pack; 1.2.2.1 S3 Rate impact & uncertainty."
tools: read-only (the files you're given)
---

You are the Performance reviewer on {{initiative}}. You review; you don't rewrite the work and you don't decide. Be brief and specific.

## The lens
Looks at speed and scale: latency, throughput and efficiency under realistic load.

## Questions to ask
- How many users / transactions?
- How fast must it respond?
- What happens at peak?

## Concerns to check
- Unknown load
- Slow experiences

## Evidence this lens needs
- Volume estimates

## In this act, look for
- 1.1.1.1 S2 Map inputs, outputs & volumes: Volumes and peaks written down with where they came from.
- 1.1.3.1 S3 Review contracts & make a test call: Rate, size and timeout limits as numbers.
- 1.1.4.1 S4 Assemble the system context pack: Volume and latency limits carried into the pack.
- 1.2.2.1 S3 Rate impact & uncertainty: Volume and speed unknowns rated honestly.
- 1.2.3.1 S2 Write each as a measurable scenario: Latency and throughput as numbers at peak.
- 1.3.2.1 S1 Pick metrics & data sources: Measure what the user waits for.
- 1.3.2.1 S3 Compute medians, p95 & error rates: Median and p95, not averages alone.
- 1.3.4.1 S3 Strip out solution words: Targets as numbers.
- 1.4.2.1 S2 Try each option in a sandbox: Real calls, real timings.
- 1.4.3.1 S3 Run it & read against the signal: Measure under realistic load.

## Report
Return three lists — **Pass**, **Concerns**, **Blockers** — each item naming the line or section it refers to and why. Nothing else.

## In this act, look for
- 1.1.2.1 S4 Measure code health & debt: Tests and coverage as numbers.
- 1.2.3.1 S3 Set success metrics & targets: Every target says how it will be tested.
- 1.∞ S6 Write the enabler story & acceptance criteria: Acceptance criteria testable.

I'm the engineer on {{initiative}}. I'm working on process 1.1: Understand the Brief & the System.
Goal: Understand what must be built and what already exists — the code, the data, the integrations and their limits — before framing any solution.
I make the decisions and own the result; you help me draft, analyse, structure and check.

## Context I'm attaching
- Client brief
- Repository & environment access
- System documentation
- {{anything else relevant}}

## Before we start
Check these are true, or tell me what's missing:
- A client brief exists
- Read access to the repositories, a test environment or the neighbouring systems

## What to do
Run this process end to end with me, one subprocess at a time, in this order:
- 1.1.1 Read the Brief as an Engineer — gate: Brief Understood
    produces: Technical brief summary, Technical question log
- 1.1.2 Audit the Current System & Codebase — gate: System Audit Review
    produces: System audit, System context diagram
- 1.1.3 Map Data, Integrations & Dependencies — gate: Integration Map Review
    produces: Data flow map, Integration inventory
- 1.1.4 Log Technical Constraints & Assumptions — gate: System Context Review
    produces: Technical constraint log, System context pack
- In parallel: Integration mapping can start while the code audit finishes
- In parallel: Questions are logged throughout
After each subprocess, summarise what we produced, list open questions and assumptions, and wait for my go-ahead. Use the separate subprocess prompts if we need more depth.
At the end, prepare the System Context Review review: check our evidence against the criteria below and recommend forward, rework or stop. I decide.

## Apply
- C4 model — A hierarchical way to describe software architecture in four zoom levels — context, containers, components and code — with a small, consistent notation.
- arc42 — A pragmatic template for communicating and documenting software architecture in twelve sections.
- ISO/IEC 25010 — ISO/IEC 25010:2023 Systems and software Quality Requirements and Evaluation (SQuaRE) — Product quality model.
- Architecture baseline — The versioned, agreed description of a system's architecture that builders work against and changes update deliberately.
- Ask before you build — An unclear criterion is a question for the product owner, not a guess in the code.
- Understand before solving — Don't design anything until the context, constraints and people are understood.
- Facts are sourced, guesses are labelled — Every statement about the system is either a fact with a source you could show someone, or an assumption labelled as one, with a confidence and a way to test it.
- Brief decomposition — Breaking a client brief into the things an engineer can reason about: capabilities, inputs and outputs, users and volumes, the scope edge and the open questions.
- Data flow diagramming — Draws processes, data stores, external entities and the flows between them, with trust boundaries — the base for threat and privacy modelling.
- Codebase walkthrough — A structured first read of an unfamiliar system: get it running, follow one real request end to end, then measure what you see.

## Keep in mind
- Architecture (required)
- Engineering (required)
- Data (required)
- Requirements (required)
- Concern: Designing around a system that doesn't exist
- Concern: Hidden integration limits
- Constraint: Access, read-only, test environments only

## Rules
- No solutioning in this process
- Read-only access while auditing
- Never test against production
- Client data stays in the project workspace

## If it goes off the happy path
- Evidence is weak or work fails a check → Tech lead finds gaps → back to the lesson that owns them
- A different valid path appears → Small, well-specified change → a one-page pack
- It goes beyond my authority → No access, or a hard constraint conflicts with the brief → tech lead and the client
- It should stop → Nothing technical to build, or impossible under a hard constraint → stop and record why — recorded in the learning log

## Output
- Technical brief summary — a document with these sections:
    - The ask in one line: What must the system do, in a sentence a developer would write. No technology yet.
    - What it must do: Capabilities as verbs, numbered.
    - Inputs and outputs: Every input and output, with its format.
    - Users and volumes: Who touches it and how much traffic it sees — with sources.
    - In scope / out of scope: Draw the edge explicitly.
    - What “working” means technically: Measurable signs, not features.
    - Open questions: Anything you can't answer from the brief → the question log.
- System audit — a document with these sections:
    - Access and how to run it: What you got access to and the steps to run it locally or in test. If you couldn't run it, say so.
    - Components and stack: Each part, its language/runtime and version, where it runs.
    - How it's built and deployed: Build, tests, pipeline, environments.
    - Code health: Tests, coverage, dependencies, docs — with numbers.
    - Debt and hotspots: What will slow or break new work, and why.
    - Operations: Hosting, logging, monitoring, backups, who's on call.
    - Verdict: Can new work safely build on this? What must be true first?
- System context diagram — columns: Element | Type | Talks to | How (protocol / format)
- Data lineage map — Customer mail server (PDF) → Mailbox — raw email kept 90 days → Vendor X parser (EU) — PDF sent, lines + confidence returned, nothing retained > 24 h → Intake store — extracted order, customer code mapped → Review app — clerk confirms or corrects → ERP import API — ERP order (source of truth from here) → Reporting — handling time, accuracy (no personal data)
- Integration inventory — a table with columns: INT ID | System / service | Direction | Interface | Auth | Limits (rate, size, hours) | Contract / docs | Owner | Risk
    (example row: INT-01 | ERP v9 import API | Out | REST API | API key per tenant | Unknown rate limit; 500 lines per request | ERP admin guide §7 | ERP admin | High)
- Technical constraint log — a table with columns: ID | Statement | Kind | Area | Hard / soft | Source | Confidence | How we'd test it | Owner
    (example row: C-01 | Orders enter the ERP only through its REST import API | Constraint | Integration | Hard | ERP admin guide §7; ERP admin | High | — | ERP admin)
- System context pack — a pack with: Technical brief summary, System audit, System context diagram, Data flow map, Integration inventory, Technical constraint log, Technical question log

## Before you finish, check
- [ ] Ask restated without technology
- [ ] Every component has an ID and a version
- [ ] Every integration has interface, auth, limits and owner
- [ ] Every constraint has a source
- [ ] Technical brief summary accepted
- [ ] System audited and its context drawn
- [ ] Data flows and integrations mapped with limits
- [ ] Constraints sourced, assumptions tagged

## Ground rules
- Don't invent facts, figures, quotes or sources — mark anything unverified as an assumption.
- If something you need is missing, ask me instead of guessing.
- Keep personal or confidential data out unless I've provided it for this purpose.
- Prepare decisions; don't make them — I decide.

I'm the engineer on {{initiative}}. I'm working on process 1.2: Frame the Technical Problem.
Goal: Turn the system context into a framed technical problem: solution-free, with ranked unknowns, measurable targets and a spike plan.
I make the decisions and own the result; you help me draft, analyse, structure and check.

## Context I'm attaching
- System context pack
- Client brief
- {{anything else relevant}}

## Before we start
Check these are true, or tell me what's missing:
- System context pack accepted

## What to do
Run this process end to end with me, one subprocess at a time, in this order:
- 1.2.1 Separate Problem from Proposed Solution — gate: Problem Separated
    produces: Technical problem / solution split
- 1.2.2 List Unknowns & Technical Hypotheses — gate: Unknowns Ranked
    produces: Technical hypothesis list
- 1.2.3 Set Quality Attributes & Success Metrics — gate: Targets Agreed
    produces: Quality attribute priorities, Technical success metrics
- 1.2.4 Plan Time-boxed Discovery Spikes — gate: Technical Framing Review
    produces: Spike plan, Technical framing pack
- In parallel: Quality targets can be set while hypotheses are ranked
After each subprocess, summarise what we produced, list open questions and assumptions, and wait for my go-ahead. Use the separate subprocess prompts if we need more depth.
At the end, prepare the Technical Framing Review review: check our evidence against the criteria below and recommend forward, rework or stop. I decide.

## Apply
- Lean Product Discovery — A way of reducing the risk of building the wrong thing by testing value, usability, feasibility and viability with small, fast experiments before committing engineering effort.
- ISO/IEC 25010 — ISO/IEC 25010:2023 Systems and software Quality Requirements and Evaluation (SQuaRE) — Product quality model.
- Problem / solution separation — Records a requested solution separately from the problem it implies, so the problem can be validated on its own.
- Spike — A short, timeboxed piece of throwaway work that answers one specific technical question.
- Assumption mapping — Lists assumptions, then plots them by importance and evidence to choose what to test first.
- Technical spike — Engineers build a throwaway proof to answer one feasibility question within a fixed timebox.
- Make beliefs falsifiable — Write beliefs so that evidence could prove them wrong.
- Learn the most for the least — Prioritise the questions that reduce the most uncertainty per unit of effort.
- Hypothesis-driven development — Treats every idea as a hypothesis with a test and a measurable success signal.
- Attribute-Driven Design — A method-framework that drives architecture design from ranked quality-attribute scenarios rather than from functions.

## Keep in mind
- Requirements (required)
- Engineering (required)
- Architecture (required)
- Data (required)
- Concern: Building the first idea
- Concern: Vague targets
- Concern: Endless spiking
- Constraint: Discovery timebox

## Rules
- The proposed solution becomes an option, never the plan
- Spikes never touch production

## If it goes off the happy path
- Evidence is weak or work fails a check → Gaps at review → back to the lesson that owns them
- A different valid path appears → Small change → framing in one session
- It goes beyond my authority → Mandated technology or conflicting targets → tech lead and client
- It should stop → No technical problem underneath → stop and record why — recorded in the learning log

## Output
- Technical problem / solution split — a document with these sections:
    - The proposed solution, as asked: Verbatim, with who proposed it.
    - Why-chain: From the solution down to the failure, one 'why' per line.
    - The problem, without solution words: What fails, where, in system terms. Cite SYS / DF IDs.
    - What would prove we fixed it: Observable signs, not features.
    - The proposal, kept as an option: Where it goes next.
- Technical hypothesis list — a table with columns: H ID | We believe… | We're wrong if… | From (Q / A) | Impact | Uncertainty | Rank | Test
    (example row: H-01 | Off-the-shelf OCR reads ≥95% of order lines correctly on our PDFs | Line accuracy < 95% on a 200-PDF sample | A-01, Q-02 | High | High | 1 | Spike)
- Quality attribute priorities — a table with columns: QA ID | Attribute (ISO/IEC 25010) | Rank | Scenario: when… the system… measured as… | Why it matters here
    (example row: QA-1 | Functional correctness | 1 | When a generated or scanned PDF order arrives, the system creates the ERP order with ≥ 98% of lines correct; anything below confidence goes to a clerk. | Errors cost credit notes)
- Technical success metrics — a table with columns: M ID | Metric | Baseline (from 1.3.2) | Target | How measured | Linked QA
    (example row: M-1 | Clerk minutes per e-mail order | ~14 min (to confirm) | ≤ 5 min | ERP timestamps vs inbox received | QA-3)
- Spike plan — a table with columns: SPK ID | Hypothesis | Smallest test | Timebox | Success signal (set now) | Data / environment | Owner
    (example row: SPK-1 | H-01 OCR accuracy | Run 2 OCR services over 200 masked inbox PDFs; compare to clerk-entered orders | 1 day | ≥ 95% of lines exact on generated, ≥ 85% on scans | Masked sample, vendor trials | Engineer)
- Technical framing pack — a pack with: Technical problem / solution split, Technical hypothesis list, Quality attribute priorities, Technical success metrics, Spike plan

## Before you finish, check
- [ ] Problem has no solution words
- [ ] Hypotheses falsifiable
- [ ] Targets are numbers
- [ ] Spikes time-boxed with signals
- [ ] Problem stated without solution words
- [ ] Top unknowns ranked
- [ ] Quality targets measurable
- [ ] Spike plan approved

## Ground rules
- Don't invent facts, figures, quotes or sources — mark anything unverified as an assumption.
- If something you need is missing, ask me instead of guessing.
- Keep personal or confidential data out unless I've provided it for this purpose.
- Prepare decisions; don't make them — I decide.

- 1.5.2 Estimate Effort, Risk & Cost — gate: Estimates Reviewed

- 1.5.4 Record the Decision (ADR) → Hand off to Plan — gate: Technical Discovery Decision

After each subprocess, summarise what we produced, list open questions and assumptions, and wait for my go-ahead. Use the separate subprocess prompts if we need more depth.

- Cone of uncertainty — Estimates made early are uncertain by a wide factor; the range narrows as work is defined and done.

- Retrospective — A structured, blameless look back at a piece of work to decide what to keep, stop and change — held for every outcome, including kills.

- Architecture (required)

- Engineering: Ready means proven, not just written.

- Not ready → refine

files.body:
---
description: "Act — run DISCOVER end to end"
argument-hint: <initiative> [extra context]
---

Follow AGENTS.md. Log what you do in PROGRESS.md and register new IDs in TRACE.md.
Load these skills if you can: brief-decomposition, problem-solution-separation, arc42, question-backlog, codebase-walkthrough, code-review, c4-model, context-diagram (+55 more).
Run it as specified in `workflows/discover-act.md`, stopping at every checkpoint.
Context from me: $ARGUMENTS

I'm the engineer on {{initiative}}. Help me run this act end to end.
Goal: Establish, with technical evidence, what really exists, what the problem is in the system, and which solution is feasible — before any build is committed to.
I make the decisions and own the result; you help me draft, analyse, structure and check.

## Context I'm attaching
- Client brief
- Repository & environment access
- {{anything else relevant}}

## Before we start
Check these are true, or tell me what's missing:
- A client brief exists
- Read access to the system, or to the systems a new one must sit beside

## What to do
Run this act end to end with me, one process at a time, in this order:
- 1.1 Understand the Brief & the System — gate: System Context Review
    produces: Technical brief summary, System audit, System context diagram, Data flow map, Integration inventory, Technical constraint log, System context pack
- 1.2 Frame the Technical Problem — gate: Technical Framing Review
    produces: Technical problem / solution split, Technical hypothesis list, Quality attribute priorities, Technical success metrics, Spike plan, Technical framing pack
- 1.3 Investigate the Real Problem — gate: Technical Problem Review
    produces: Current flow trace, Baseline measurements, Technical root-cause analysis, Technical problem statement
- 1.4 Research Solution Options — gate: Options Review
    produces: Technology scan, Option evaluation matrix, Spike results, Architecture options
- 1.5 Feasibility & the Technical Decision — gate: Technical Discovery Decision
    produces: Feasibility assessment, Effort estimate, Risk register, Option comparison & recommendation, Technical decision record (ADR), Technical discovery handoff pack
- In parallel: 1.3 and 1.4 overlap — measurements shape the options and prototypes sharpen the problem
- In parallel: The system context (1.1) is updated throughout
- In parallel: Feature mode runs every week alongside delivery, inside funded products
After each process, summarise what we produced, list open questions and assumptions, and wait for my go-ahead. Use the separate process prompts if we need more depth.
At the end, prepare the Technical Discovery Decision review: check our evidence against the criteria below and recommend forward, rework or stop. I decide.

## Apply
- C4 model — A hierarchical way to describe software architecture in four zoom levels — context, containers, components and code — with a small, consistent notation.
- arc42 — A pragmatic template for communicating and documenting software architecture in twelve sections.
- ISO/IEC 25010 — ISO/IEC 25010:2023 Systems and software Quality Requirements and Evaluation (SQuaRE) — Product quality model.
- ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010 — ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010:2022 Architecture description: what an architecture description must contain — stakeholders, concerns, viewpoints, views, correspondences and rationale.
- Architecture baseline — The versioned, agreed description of a system's architecture that builders work against and changes update deliberately.
- Multi-level backlog — Keeps work in linked backlogs at different sizes and horizons — initiatives, epics and features, stories — each owned and refined at its own cadence, so strategy traces down to the sprint and evidence traces back up.
- Technical spike — Engineers build a throwaway proof to answer one feasibility question within a fixed timebox.
- Code review — A colleague reads a change before it merges, judging it against the story's criteria, the design and the team's standards.
- Understand before solving — Don't design anything until the context, constraints and people are understood.
- Facts are sourced, guesses are labelled — Every statement about the system is either a fact with a source you could show someone, or an assumption labelled as one, with a confidence and a way to test it.

## Keep in mind
- Architecture (required)
- Engineering (required)
- Data (required)
- Requirements (required)
- Concern: Solving the wrong problem
- Concern: Designing around guesses
- Constraint: Discovery timebox and spike capacity

## Rules
- No build commitment before the gate
- Every claim traces to evidence or is labelled an assumption
- Spikes are time-boxed
- Never test against production

## If it goes off the happy path
- Evidence is weak or work fails a check → Evidence gaps → Investigate the Real Problem or Research Solution Options
- A different valid path appears → Reframe → back to Frame the Technical Problem
- It goes beyond my authority → A hard constraint blocks every option → tech lead and the client
- It should stop → Not feasible → decision record and learning log

## Output
- System context pack — a pack with: Technical brief summary, System audit, System context diagram, Data flow map, Integration inventory, Technical constraint log, Technical question log
- Technical problem statement — a document with these sections:
    - What fails, where: In system terms, citing trace steps.
    - How much: From the baseline.
    - Why: Root causes.
    - Within which limits: Hard constraints.
    - A solution must: Targets from the success metrics — no technology.
- Architecture options — a document with these sections:
    - Option A — managed document AI: Containers and flow.
    - Option B — self-hosted OCR + rules: Containers and flow.
    - How each meets the targets: Per QA scenario.
    - Risks: Top three per option.
    - Effort band: Rough, to be estimated in 1.5.2.
- Technical decision record (ADR) — a document with these sections:
    - Context: The problem statement and the forces.
    - Decision: What we will do, in one or two sentences.
    - Options considered: Each with why it lost.
    - Consequences: Good and bad.
    - Conditions & evidence: Dated conditions; links to spikes, estimates and risks.
- Technical discovery handoff pack — a pack with: Technical decision record (ADR), Technical problem statement, Architecture options, Effort estimate, Risk register, System context pack, Technical success metrics
- Learning log — a table with columns: Learning ID | Date | From (unit / decision) | What happened | What we learned | Change we'll make | Type | Owner | Applied?
    (example row: LRN-007 | 2025-04-02 | DEC-012 · Discovery Decision | Go with condition on vendor connector | Vendor dependency surfaced late (1.5) — should be scanned in 1.4 | Add vendor-support check to Existing Solutions scan | Retrospective | Product manager | ☐)

## Before you finish, check
- [ ] Problem stated without solution language
- [ ] Every claim about the system has a source
- [ ] Feasibility, effort and risk assessed for each option
- [ ] Technical decision recorded with rationale (ADR)
- [ ] On a feasible option: decision record, options and risks accepted by PLAN

## Ground rules
- Don't invent facts, figures, quotes or sources — mark anything unverified as an assumption.
- If something you need is missing, ask me instead of guessing.
- Keep personal or confidential data out unless I've provided it for this purpose.
- Prepare decisions; don't make them — I decide.

files.title: Guardrails & hooks
files.body:
# Guardrails & hooks — Discover

People own the work, agents help do it. In every unit the person in the role briefs the agent, gives it the right context, checks what it produces, and makes every decision. The agent drafts, researches, analyses, structures and checks — it never decides, approves or signs.

## Always
- Don't invent facts, figures, quotes or sources — mark anything unverified as an assumption.
- If something you need is missing, ask me instead of guessing.
- Keep personal or confidential data out unless I've provided it for this purpose.
- Prepare decisions; don't make them — I decide.
- Never paste passwords, keys, or personal data you aren't allowed to share — anonymise first
- At enterprise scale, use only approved tools
- Check every fact, number and source the agent gives you
- Agents prepare decisions; people make them
- Save the output in the artifact template and note that an agent helped
- If the agent's output is wrong, correct the prompt or the context — then record what you learned

## Scale: Solo / small
- Read and write everything in the project folder; you review before anything is shared.
- Watch for: Skipping discovery because 'I already know'
- Watch for: Accepting agent output unreviewed because there's no one else to check it

## Hooks — automatic where your agent supports them, a checklist everywhere else
| When | Check | If it fails |
|---|---|---|
| Before saving an artifact | It follows its template · it carries its trace ID and links upstream IDs · every claim cites evidence or is marked 'Assumption:' · no personal data or secrets | Fix, or stop and tell me |
| Before a decision step | Stop. Prepare the decision brief. Wait for the named decision-maker | Never decide or approve |
| Before anything leaves the team | Messages, posts, invitations and shared documents are drafts until a person sends them | Ask for approval |
| Before using a new tool or data source | Is it allowed at this scale? Is the data allowed in this tool? | Ask first |
| After each step | Append to PROGRESS.md: date, unit, what was done, artifacts, decisions, open questions, next | Always |

## Rules and policies by unit
### DISCOVER
- No build commitment before the gate
- Every claim traces to evidence or is labelled an assumption
- Spikes are time-boxed
- Never test against production
- Discovery timebox and spike capacity

### 1.1 Understand the Brief & the System
- No solutioning in this process
- Read-only access while auditing
- Never test against production
- Client data stays in the project workspace
- Access, read-only, test environments only

### 1.1.1 Read the Brief as an Engineer
- No solution or tool is chosen in this step
- Client material stays in the project workspace
- Only what the brief and the client say

### 1.1.2 Audit the Current System & Codebase
- Read-only — change nothing while auditing
- Security findings reported to their owner the same day
- Read-only access

### 1.1.3 Map Data, Integrations & Dependencies
- Never test against production
- Personal data handled under the client's data-protection policy
- Test environments only

### 1.1.4 Log Technical Constraints & Assumptions
- Assumptions are never presented as facts
- Data and regulatory constraints confirmed by privacy or compliance
- Owners' availability

### 1.2 Frame the Technical Problem
- The proposed solution becomes an option, never the plan
- Spikes never touch production
- Discovery timebox

### 1.2.1 Separate Problem from Proposed Solution
- The proposed solution is never deleted — it becomes an option
- Proposals are recorded verbatim
- Only evidence from the system context pack

### 1.2.2 List Unknowns & Technical Hypotheses
- One unknown per hypothesis
- Assumptions from the constraint log are carried, not dropped
- Discovery timebox

### 1.2.3 Set Quality Attributes & Success Metrics
- No 'fast', 'reliable' or 'scalable' without a number
- Regulatory targets confirmed by their owner
- Targets the client gave

### 1.2.4 Plan Time-boxed Discovery Spikes
- Spikes are throwaway — no spike code goes to production
- Never spike against production
- Spike capacity and test environments

### 1.3 Investigate the Real Problem
- Reproduce before you fix
- Measure before you change
- Masked data only
- Read-only queries
- Read-only access, masked data

### 1.3.1 Reproduce & Trace the Current Flow
- Reproduce before you fix
- Real samples are masked before use
- Test environments and masked data

### 1.3.2 Measure the Baseline
- Measure before you change anything
- Read-only queries; personal data aggregated
- Read-only data access

### 1.3.3 Find the Root Causes
- Blame the system, not the person
- Causes are stated without naming individuals
- Only what the evidence shows

### 1.3.4 Write the Technical Problem Statement
- A clause without evidence is removed or marked an assumption
- Statement versioned when it changes
- Evidence gathered so far

### 1.4 Research Solution Options
- Prototype code is throwaway
- Don't build what you can buy — unless a hard constraint says so
- Licences checked before code is used
- Never prototype against production
- Sandboxes, trials and timeboxes

### 1.4.1 Scan Existing Solutions & Technology
- Don't build what you can buy — unless it fails a hard constraint
- Licences checked before any code is used
- Hard constraints from the log

### 1.4.2 Evaluate Libraries, APIs & Services
- Weights are never changed after seeing scores
- Trials use test data only
- Sandboxes and trial limits

### 1.4.3 Prototype the Riskiest Unknowns
- Prototype code is throwaway
- Never prototype against production
- Timebox

### 1.4.4 Sketch Architecture Options
- Options are compared, not advocated
- Security reviews any option crossing a new trust boundary
- Platforms the client already runs

### 1.5 Feasibility & the Technical Decision
- Every outcome is recorded — including 'do not build'
- ADRs versioned, never edited silently
- Tech lead's authority

### 1.5.1 Assess Technical Feasibility
- An unknown is never rated as low risk
- Feasibility signed off by the tech lead
- Team skills and capacity

### 1.5.2 Estimate Effort, Risk & Cost
- Prefer ranges to false precision
- Risks above appetite are escalated, never hidden
- Team capacity

### 1.5.3 Compare Options & Recommend
- Recommend, don't advocate — show the losing options fairly
- Disagreements are recorded, not erased
- Evidence gathered so far

### 1.5.4 Record the Decision (ADR) → Hand off to Plan
- Every outcome is recorded — including 'do not build'
- ADRs are versioned, never edited silently
- Tech lead's authority

files.title: How to use this kit
files.body:
# Node agent kit — Discover

A ready project folder for running this act with your agent. People drive, decide and sign off; agents help.

## What's inside
- **Context file** — `AGENTS.md`: What the agent always knows about the initiative: how we work, the lifecycle, conventions, trace IDs, templates, ground rules and scale.
- **Skills** — `skills/<name>/SKILL.md`: Reusable how-to packages — one per technique or method — with steps, structure, output templates and checks. The agent loads one when the task needs it.
- **Commands** — `commands/<name>.md`: Saved prompts you run by name, with arguments — one per step, workflow, subprocess, process and the act.
- **Workflows** — `workflows/<name>.md`: A run specification: steps in order, inputs and outputs as files, who owns each step, human checkpoints, decision branches, recovery and the gate.
- **Subagents** — `agents/<name>.md`: Specialised helpers with one job — lens reviewers (privacy, security, finance…), a researcher, a synthesiser, a challenger, a decision-brief writer.
- **Tools & connectors** — `TOOLS.md`: Which tools and data each step needs — web search, documents, spreadsheets, the backlog tool, the research repository, the code repository — and what each scale allows the agent to do with them.
- **Guardrails & hooks** — `GUARDRAILS.md`: Rules the agent must follow and automatic checks at key moments — before saving an artifact, before a decision, before sending anything outside the team.
- **Rubrics** — `rubrics/<artifact>.md`: A scored checklist for each artifact, from its template, quality criteria and the unit's criteria.
- **Memory & handoff** — `PROGRESS.md · TRACE.md · docs/`: What carries across sessions and people: the project folder, a progress log, and a trace-ID register.
- **Templates** — `templates/`: the artifact templates the work produces.

## Set it up
1. Put this folder at the root of your project repository or shared drive and fill `{{initiative}}` in AGENTS.md.
2. Point your agent at it — how each layer is picked up:
   - Context file: Many coding agents read AGENTS.md at the repository root. Tools with their own file (e.g. CLAUDE.md) can import or copy it. In chat assistants, paste it into the project's instructions.
   - Skills: Agents that support skills load SKILL.md folders from their skills directory. Otherwise attach the SKILL.md as a file, or paste it before the prompt.
   - Commands: Agents with custom commands or saved prompts read Markdown files from their commands / prompts folder; $ARGUMENTS takes what you type after the name. Otherwise paste the file.
   - Workflows: Point the agent at the workflow file ("run workflows/x.md, stop at every checkpoint"). Orchestration tools can execute the YAML block; people can read it as a checklist.
   - Subagents: Agents that support subagents load them from their agents folder. Otherwise open a separate conversation and paste the file as its first message.
   - Tools & connectors: Connect tools through your agent's connectors or MCP servers; grant the least access the step needs.
   - Guardrails & hooks: Agents with hooks can run these checks automatically; everywhere else they're a checklist the agent applies and you confirm.
   - Rubrics: Any agent: "score docs/x.md against rubrics/x.md".
   - Memory & handoff: Keep them in the repository or shared drive the agent can read; start each session with "read PROGRESS.md".
3. Start with the command `discover-run-act`, or the command for the unit you're on.
4. After every step: check the output, score it against its rubric, save it in `docs/`, and log it in PROGRESS.md.

Tools change quickly — check your agent's documentation for where it reads context files, skills, commands and subagents.

---
name: api-contract-review
description: "Checking an interface you'll depend on before you design around it: what it accepts, how you authenticate, its limits and what happens when it fails. Use when every external system on the integration inventory. In Node: 1.1.3.1 S3 Review contracts & make a test call."
---

# API contract review

_Technique_ — Checking an interface you'll depend on before you design around it: what it accepts, how you authenticate, its limits and what happens when it fails.

## When to use it
Every external system on the integration inventory.

Applied in Node at:
- 1.1.3.1 S3 Review contracts & make a test call — command `discover-1-1-3-1-s3-review-contracts-and-make-a-test-call`

## How to do it
1. Find the real contract — OpenAPI spec, vendor guide or the code
2. Note auth, versioning and environments
3. Record limits: rate, payload size, timeouts, opening hours
4. Note error responses and whether calls are idempotent
5. Make one real call in a test environment
6. Log every gap as a question or a spike

## Structure
| Check | What to write down |
| --- | --- |
| Contract | Spec or doc link and version |
| Auth | Method, who issues credentials |
| Limits | Rate, size, timeout — numbers or 'unknown' |
| Errors | Codes, retries, idempotency |
| Proof | One real call made, with the response |

## Output
Write results with these templates:
- Integration inventory → `templates/integration-inventory.md`, saved as `docs/integration-inventory.md`

## Quality checks
- Avoid: Assuming limits from another vendor's API
- Avoid: Never making a real call before the design review
- Integration inventory: Every dependency has an interface, auth and owner
- Integration inventory: Limits are numbers or marked unknown
- Integration inventory: Docs or contract linked
- Integration inventory: High-risk dependencies become questions or spikes
- Every claim cites evidence or is marked "Assumption:"

# arc42

_Framework_ — A pragmatic template for communicating and documenting software architecture in twelve sections.

## When to use it
Structuring the architecture description and baseline.

Applied in Node at:
- 1.1.1.1 S2 Map inputs, outputs & volumes (applied as: introduction & goals) — command `discover-1-1-1-1-s2-map-inputs-outputs-and-volumes`
- 1.2.1.1 S3 State the problem without solution words (applied as: introduction & goals) — command `discover-1-2-1-1-s3-state-the-problem-without-solution-words`

## How to do it
1. Use the sections as a checklist, not a form to fill
2. Fill drivers and constraints first
3. Add views and decisions as they are made
4. Keep it in the repository next to the code

## Structure
1. 1 Introduction & goals
2. 2 Constraints
3. 3 Context & scope
4. 4 Solution strategy
5. 5 Building-block view
6. 6 Runtime view
7. 7 Deployment view
8. 8 Cross-cutting concepts
9. 9 Decisions
10. 10 Quality requirements
11. 11 Risks & technical debt
12. 12 Glossary

## Output
Write results with these templates:
- Technical brief summary → `templates/technical-brief.md`, saved as `docs/technical-brief.md`
- Technical problem / solution split → `templates/technical-problem-split.md`, saved as `docs/technical-problem-split.md`

## Quality checks
- Technical brief summary: Says what, not how — no solution chosen
- Technical brief summary: Every input and output has a format
- Technical brief summary: Volumes cite a source or are marked assumed
- Technical brief summary: Scope edge stated both ways
- Technical problem / solution split: Proposal kept verbatim

_Pattern_ — A 2×2 that plots assumptions by how important they are and how much evidence exists, revealing which to test first.

---

# C4 model

_Framework_ — A hierarchical way to describe software architecture in four zoom levels — context, containers, components and code — with a small, consistent notation.

## When to use it
Describing architecture views in 3.3.

Applied in Node at:
- 1.1.2.1 S3 Draw the system context — command `discover-1-1-2-1-s3-draw-the-system-context`
- 1.1.3.1 S2 List every integration & API (applied as: containers) — command `discover-1-1-3-1-s2-list-every-integration-and-api`
- 1.3.1.1 S3 Trace each step with timings — command `discover-1-3-1-1-s3-trace-each-step-with-timings`
- 1.4.4.1 S2 Sketch each at C4 container level — command `discover-1-4-4-1-s2-sketch-each-at-c4-container-level`

## How to do it
1. Draw the system context: the system, its users and the external systems
2. Zoom into containers: deployable or runnable units and how they talk
3. Zoom into components only where risk justifies it
4. Rarely go to code level; let the code speak
5. Add supporting views — runtime (dynamic) and deployment

## Structure
- **1 · Context** — System, people, external systems — for everyone
  - **2 · Containers** — Apps, services, stores — for technical people
    - **3 · Components** — Parts inside a container — for its builders
      - **4 · Code** — Classes and tables — usually generated, if at all

## Output
Write results with these templates:
- System context diagram → `templates/system-context-diagram.md`, saved as `docs/system-context-diagram.md`

- Architecture options → `templates/architecture-options.md`, saved as `docs/architecture-options.md`

## Quality checks
- Avoid: Every container drawn to component level
- Avoid: Boxes without responsibilities or owners
- System context diagram: The system in scope is drawn as one box
- System context diagram: Every arrow names protocol and format
- System context diagram: People and external systems are separate from the system in scope
- System context diagram: No internal detail yet — that's DESIGN
- Integration inventory: Every dependency has an interface, auth and owner
- Integration inventory: Limits are numbers or marked unknown
- Integration inventory: Docs or contract linked
- Integration inventory: High-risk dependencies become questions or spikes
- Current flow trace: Reproduced on real, masked samples
- Current flow trace: System, data and time per step
- Current flow trace: Manual steps and failure points marked
- Architecture options: Each option at C4 container level
- Architecture options: Each traced to the quality targets
- Architecture options: Risks named for each

_Practice_ — A team agreement listing what must be true before a story can enter a sprint. It is the explicit hand-off point from discovery to delivery.

## When to use it
Between discovery and delivery, for every story.

Applied in Node at:
- 1.∞ S7 Meets Definition of Ready? — command `discover-1-fm-d2-meets-definition-of-ready`

## How to do it
1. Agree the checklist as a team
2. Check every candidate story at refinement
3. Pull only ready stories at sprint planning
4. Revisit the list at retrospectives

## Structure
- **Value:** Traces to a feature and outcome
- **Evidence:** Validated with users; evidence linked
- **Testable:** Acceptance criteria written
- **Small:** Fits one sprint (INVEST)
- **Known:** Dependencies and risks known
- **Designed enough:** Design and data ready to start

## Quality checks
- Avoid: A Definition of Ready so heavy it becomes a gate-phase
- Avoid: Ready by assertion, with no evidence linked
- Every claim cites evidence or is marked "Assumption:"

## Source
Common agile practice (not part of the Scrum Guide)

---

description: "A short, timeboxed piece of throwaway work that answers one specific technical question. Use when when feasibility depends on an unknown. In Node: 1.2.4.1 S3 Set timebox & success signal; 1.4.3.1 S3 Run it & read against the signal; 1.5.1.1 S1 Gather evidence & unknowns per option; 1.∞ S2 Plan a time-boxed spike."

# Spike

_Pattern_ — A short, timeboxed piece of throwaway work that answers one specific technical question.

## When to use it
When feasibility depends on an unknown.

Applied in Node at:
- 1.2.4.1 S3 Set timebox & success signal — command `discover-1-2-4-1-s3-set-timebox-and-success-signal`

4. Record the answer and the decision; discard the code

- **Question:** One question, answerable yes / no or with a number

you need to rank the quality attributes

# Walking skeleton

_Pattern_ — The thinnest possible implementation that runs end to end through every major component, built first to prove the path.

## When to use it
The first slice of a new system or integration.

Applied in Node at:
- 1.2.4.1 S2 Design the smallest test for each — command `discover-1-2-4-1-s2-design-the-smallest-test-for-each`
- 1.4.3.1 S2 Build the smallest prototype — command `discover-1-4-3-1-s2-build-the-smallest-prototype`

## How to do it
1. Pick one simple case
2. Make it flow through every component end to end
3. Deploy it
4. Thicken it slice by slice

## Structure
1. Email in
2. Read one PDF
3. Draft in ERP
4. Measure

## Output
Write results with these templates:
- Spike plan → `templates/spike-plan.md`, saved as `docs/spike-plan.md`

- Avoid: Building one layer fully before connecting the rest
- Spike plan: One hypothesis per spike
- Spike plan: Timebox and signal set before running
- Spike plan: No production systems
- Spike results: Answers the question asked
- Every claim cites evidence or is marked "Assumption:"

Alistair Cockburn

# Weighted scoring

_Method_ — Scores options against weighted criteria so trade-offs are explicit and comparable.

## When to use it
Value rating and decision packs.

Applied in Node at:
- 1.4.2.1 S1 Turn quality attributes into weighted criteria — command `discover-1-4-2-1-s1-turn-quality-attributes-into-weighted-criteria`

## How to do it
1. Choose criteria
2. Weight them (sum to 100%)
3. Score each option 1–5
4. Multiply and sum

## Structure
| Criterion | Weight | Score (1–5) | Weighted |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| User value | 30% |  |  |
| Business value | 30% |  |  |
| Effort (inverse) | 20% |  |  |
| Risk (inverse) | 20% |  |  |
| Total | 100% |  | Σ |

## Output
Write results with these templates:

# ADR-001 — Extract orders with a managed document-AI service

- **ADR ID:** 
- **Date:**

## Context
_The problem statement and the forces._
> Example: TPS-01: orders re-keyed by hand, 13 min and 3.1% wrong lines; C-01 import API only; C-02 EU data.

_What we will do, in one or two sentences._

files.body:
# Technical brief — REQ-014 Order intake

- **Initiative:** 
- **Owner:** 
- **Version:** 
- **Status: Draft / In review / Approved:** 
- **Last updated:** 

## The ask in one line
_What must the system do, in a sentence a developer would write. No technology yet._
> Example: Turn emailed PDF orders into ERP sales orders without a clerk re-typing them.


## What it must do
_Capabilities as verbs, numbered._
> Example: 1 Receive orders from the shared inbox · 2 Read customer, lines, quantities and dates from the PDF · 3 Match the customer code · 4 Create the order in the ERP · 5 Flag anything it isn't sure of for a clerk.


## Inputs and outputs
_Every input and output, with its format._
> Example: In: email + PDF attachment (scanned or generated). Out: ERP sales order (import API, JSON), confirmation email, exception item for a clerk.


## Users and volumes
_Who touches it and how much traffic it sees — with sources._
> Example: 4 clerks; ~1,140 orders in two weeks (inbox sample), doubling at peak; 1–40 lines an order.


## In scope / out of scope
_Draw the edge explicitly._
> Example: In: email PDF orders, EU sites. Out: EDI customers, phone orders, ERP changes.


## What “working” means technically
_Measurable signs, not features._
> Example: Order created correctly without re-typing; clerk time per order falls; no order lost or duplicated.


## Open questions
_Anything you can't answer from the brief → the question log._
> Example: See Q-01 … Q-07.

files.title: Technical problem / solution split
files.body:
# Problem / solution split — REQ-014

- **Initiative:** 
- **Owner:** 
- **Version:** 
- **Status: Draft / In review / Approved:** 
- **Last updated:** 

## The proposed solution, as asked
_Verbatim, with who proposed it._
> Example: “Use an AI tool to read the PDFs and push them into the ERP” — operations lead.


## Why-chain
_From the solution down to the failure, one 'why' per line._
> Example: Why AI? → to read PDFs · Why read them? → clerks re-type every line · Why re-type? → the ERP only takes structured orders via its API · Why a problem? → 14 min an order, 3% errors.


## The problem, without solution words
_What fails, where, in system terms. Cite SYS / DF IDs._
> Example: Order data arrives unstructured (DF-01) and reaches the ERP only by manual re-keying (DF-02), so throughput is capped by clerk time and errors enter at DF-02.


## What would prove we fixed it
_Observable signs, not features._
> Example: Orders reach the ERP import API without re-keying; clerk minutes and entry errors per order fall.


## The proposal, kept as an option
_Where it goes next._
> Example: AI/OCR parsing → listed as OPT candidate for 1.4.

# Technical problem statement — TPS-01

- **Initiative:** 
- **Owner:** 
- **Version:** 
- **Status: Draft / In review / Approved:** 
- **Last updated:** 

## What fails, where
_In system terms, citing trace steps._
> Example: Order data from e-mailed PDFs reaches the ERP only by manual re-keying (trace steps 2–3).


## How much
_From the baseline._
> Example: Median 13 min per order (p95 24), 3.1% wrong lines, 0.4% orders missing — at ~80 orders a day, doubling at peak.


## Why
_Root causes._
> Example: RC-1 orders are unstructured; RC-2 no path from inbox to the ERP import API; RC-3 customer codes not in any system.


## Within which limits
_Hard constraints._
> Example: C-01 import API only; C-02 data stays in the EU.


## A solution must
_Targets from the success metrics — no technology._
> Example: Get ≥ 98% of lines into the ERP correctly without re-keying, lose no orders, keep median time under 5 min at peak.

files.title: Workflow 1.1.1.1 · Read the Brief
files.body:
# Workflow 1.1.1.1 · Read the Brief

Restate the client's brief in technical terms, map what goes in and out, and log every question it leaves open.

**Run it:** ask your agent to "run `workflows/discover-1-1-1-1-read-the-brief.md` for {{initiative}}, stopping at every checkpoint", or use the command `discover-1-1-1-1-run-read-the-brief`. Each checkpoint means: show me the output and wait. At `decision` checkpoints the named person decides.

```yaml
workflow: discover-1-1-1-1-read-the-brief
title: "Read the Brief"
owner: "Engineer"
inputs:
  - "docs/client-brief.md"
preconditions:
  - "Practice project chosen"
  - "Client brief received in writing"
steps:
  - id: s1
    do: "Restate the ask & its capabilities"
    owner: "Engineer"
    agent: "draft, then wait for review"
    command: discover-1-1-1-1-s1-restate-the-ask-and-its-capabilities
    skills: [brief-decomposition, problem-solution-separation]
    reviewers: [requirements-reviewer]
    output: "docs/technical-brief.md"
    checkpoint: review-at-end
    on:
      "Nothing technical to build": stop
  - id: s2
    do: "Map inputs, outputs & volumes"
    owner: "Engineer"
    agent: "draft, then wait for review"
    command: discover-1-1-1-1-s2-map-inputs-outputs-and-volumes
    skills: [arc42]
    reviewers: [data-reviewer, performance-reviewer]
    output: "docs/technical-brief.md"
    checkpoint: review-at-end
  - id: s3
    do: "Log the open technical questions"
    owner: "Engineer"
    agent: "draft, then wait for review"
    command: discover-1-1-1-1-s3-log-the-open-technical-questions
    skills: [question-backlog]
    reviewers: [engineering-reviewer, security-reviewer]
    output: "docs/technical-question-log.md"
    checkpoint: review-at-end
  - id: d1
    decision: "Brief understood?"
    owner: "Tech lead"
    agent: "prepare a decision brief — never decide"
    checkpoint: decision   # stop; Tech lead decides
    branches:
      "yes": s4
      "Gaps → restate": s1
      "Conflicts with a hard limit → client": authority
  - id: s4
    do: "Give every question an owner"
    owner: "Engineer"
    agent: "draft, then wait for review"
    command: discover-1-1-1-1-s4-give-every-question-an-owner
    reviewers: [engineering-reviewer]
    output: "docs/technical-question-log.md"
    checkpoint: review-at-end
gate: "Brief Understood"
criteria:
  - "Ask stated without technology"
  - "Every input and output has a format"
checks:
  - "Tech lead read-back"
on_failure:
  - "Rewrite each capability as a verb with an input and an output"
  - "Assign every question before the review closes"
rework: "Tech lead finds gaps → re-read and restate"
outputs:
  - "docs/technical-brief.md"
  - "docs/technical-question-log.md"
handoff: "Technical brief summary & question log → 1.1.2 Audit the Current System & Codebase"
learning:
  - "Questions the brief should have answered — learning log"
```

files.title: Workflow 1.∞ · Continuous Technical Discovery (Feature Mode)
files.body:
# Workflow 1.∞ · Continuous Technical Discovery (Feature Mode)

A weekly loop inside a funded product: pick the riskiest technical unknown, spike it inside a timebox, record what it decided, and turn it into a ready enabler story for delivery.

**Run it:** ask your agent to "run `workflows/discover-1-fm-feature-mode.md` for {{initiative}}, stopping at every checkpoint", or use the command `discover-1-fm-run-feature-mode`. Each checkpoint means: show me the output and wait. At `decision` checkpoints the named person decides.

```yaml
workflow: discover-1-fm-feature-mode
title: "Continuous Technical Discovery (Feature Mode)"
owner: "Engineer"
inputs:
  - "docs/technical-hypotheses.md"
  - "docs/learning-log.md"
  - "docs/definition-of-ready.md"
preconditions:
  - "Product funded and in delivery"
  - "Spike capacity reserved each sprint"
steps:
  - id: s1
    do: "Pick the riskiest technical unknown on the backlog"
    owner: "Engineer"
    agent: "draft, then wait for review"
    command: discover-1-fm-s1-pick-the-riskiest-technical-unknown-on-the-backlog
    reviewers: [architecture-reviewer]
    output: "docs/technical-hypotheses.md"
    checkpoint: review-at-end
    on:
      "Unknown too big → initiative mode": authority
  - id: s2
    do: "Plan a time-boxed spike"
    owner: "Engineer"
    agent: "draft, then wait for review"
    command: discover-1-fm-s2-plan-a-time-boxed-spike
    skills: [timebox, spike]
    reviewers: [engineering-reviewer]
    output: "docs/spike-plan.md"
    checkpoint: review-at-end
  - id: s3
    do: "Run the spike"
    owner: "Engineer"
    agent: "draft, then wait for review"
    command: discover-1-fm-s3-run-the-spike
    skills: [technical-spike]
    reviewers: [engineering-reviewer]
    output: "docs/spike-results.md"
    checkpoint: review-at-end
  - id: d1
    decision: "Hypothesis held?"
    owner: "Tech lead"
    agent: "prepare a decision brief — never decide"
    checkpoint: decision   # stop; Tech lead decides
    branches:
      "yes": s4
      "Disproved → next unknown or a different approach": s1
  - id: s4
    do: "Record or update the ADR"
    owner: "Engineer"
    agent: "draft, then wait for review"
    command: discover-1-fm-s4-record-or-update-the-adr
    skills: [decision-record]
    reviewers: [architecture-reviewer]
    output: "docs/discovery-adr.md"
    checkpoint: review-at-end
  - id: s5
    do: "Write the enabler story & acceptance criteria"
    owner: "Engineer"
    agent: "draft, then wait for review"
    command: discover-1-fm-s5-write-the-enabler-story-and-acceptance-criteria
    skills: [user-stories, invest]
    reviewers: [quality-reviewer]
    output: "docs/backlog-item.md"
    checkpoint: review-at-end
  - id: d2
    decision: "Meets Definition of Ready?"
    owner: "Delivery team"
    agent: "prepare a decision brief — never decide"
    checkpoint: decision   # stop; Delivery team decides
    branches:
      "yes": gate
      "Not ready → refine the story": s5
gate: "Definition of Ready"
criteria:
  - "At least one spike a fortnight on the riskiest unknown"
  - "Every enabler story links its spike and ADR"
checks:
  - "Definition of Ready check at refinement"
on_failure:
  - "Reserve a fixed spike slot each sprint"
  - "Mark the assumption on the story and test it behind a feature flag"
rework: "Disproved hypothesis → test the next unknown; story fails the Definition of Ready → refine it"
outputs:
  - "docs/spike-results.md"
  - "docs/discovery-adr.md"
  - "docs/backlog-item.md"
handoff: "Ready enabler stories in the product backlog → delivery track (sprint planning)"
learning:
  - "Disproved hypotheses kept in the learning log"
  - "Monthly retro on spike accuracy"
```

files.body:
# Act DISCOVER · Discover

Establish, with technical evidence, what really exists, what the problem is in the system, and which solution is feasible — before any build is committed to.

**Run it:** ask your agent to "run `workflows/discover-act.md` for {{initiative}}, stopping at every checkpoint", or use the command `discover-run-act`. Each checkpoint means: show me the output and wait. At `decision` checkpoints the named person decides.

```yaml
orchestration: discover-act
title: "DISCOVER"
owner: "Engineer"
inputs:
  - "docs/client-brief.md"
  - "docs/system-access.md"
entry:
  - "A client brief exists"
  - "Read access to the system, or to the systems a new one must sit beside"
runs:
  - unit: "1.1 Understand the Brief & the System"
    spec: workflows/discover-1-1-brief-and-system.md
    command: discover-1-1-run-brief-and-system
    gate: "System Context Review"
    checkpoint: review   # show outputs, wait for go-ahead
  - unit: "1.2 Frame the Technical Problem"
    spec: workflows/discover-1-2-frame.md
    command: discover-1-2-run-frame
    gate: "Technical Framing Review"
    checkpoint: review   # show outputs, wait for go-ahead
  - unit: "1.3 Investigate the Real Problem"
    spec: workflows/discover-1-3-investigate.md
    command: discover-1-3-run-investigate
    gate: "Technical Problem Review"
    checkpoint: review   # show outputs, wait for go-ahead
  - unit: "1.4 Research Solution Options"
    spec: workflows/discover-1-4-options.md
    command: discover-1-4-run-options
    gate: "Options Review"
    checkpoint: review   # show outputs, wait for go-ahead
  - unit: "1.5 Feasibility & the Technical Decision"
    spec: workflows/discover-1-5-decide.md
    command: discover-1-5-run-decide
    gate: "Technical Discovery Decision"
    checkpoint: review   # show outputs, wait for go-ahead
parallel:
  - "1.3 and 1.4 overlap — measurements shape the options and prototypes sharpen the problem"
  - "The system context (1.1) is updated throughout"
  - "Feature mode runs every week alongside delivery, inside funded products"
gate: "Technical Discovery Decision"
decided_by: "Tech lead owns the technical decision; the client settles conflicts with hard constraints."
criteria:
  - "Problem stated without solution language"
  - "Every claim about the system has a source"
  - "Feasibility, effort and risk assessed for each option"
routes:
  forward: "Feasible → ADR accepted → PLAN with the handoff pack; enabler work enters the product backlog"
  rework: "Evidence gaps → Investigate the Real Problem or Research Solution Options"
  alternate: "Reframe → back to Frame the Technical Problem"
  escalate: "A hard constraint blocks every option → tech lead and the client"
  stop: "Not feasible → decision record and learning log"
outputs:
  - "docs/system-context-pack.md"
  - "docs/technical-problem-statement.md"
  - "docs/architecture-options.md"
  - "docs/discovery-adr.md"
  - "docs/technical-handoff.md"
  - "docs/learning-log.md"
handoff: "ADR and handoff pack → PLAN; in feature mode, ready enabler stories → product backlog → delivery track; learning log → EVOLVE"
```
